title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: Control flow means deciding which step runs next. In which design of the makerspace assistant does the program's code, not the model, own the control flow?

options.text: The model chooses one of three tools each turn and decides when to stop
The model reads each tool result and decides which tool to call next
Code always runs search_manuals, then hands the pages to the model to write the answer
The model plans its own sequence of tool calls and ends the loop when done

items.stem: Every booking request follows the same steps: check the calendar, book the slot if it is free, then send a confirmation. The steps and their order are known in advance. How should you build this part of the assistant?

options.text: As an agent, because it calls tools, and any system that calls tools is an agent
As a fixed workflow, because the steps and their order are known ahead of time
As an agent, because letting the model choose each step is always more reliable
As a fixed workflow, because a workflow never needs to call a language model

items.stem: In one sentence, what is the difference between a workflow and an agent?

Booking requests can be handled by a fixed workflow that makes exactly 2 model calls per request, or by an agent that averages 5 model calls per request. Assume every model call costs $0.01. For 200 requests, how much more does the agent cost than the workflow, in dollars?
Which request to the makerspace assistant best justifies using an agent rather than a fixed workflow?

options.text: "Cancel my booking, number 4471", which always means look it up, then delete it
"What are the makerspace's opening hours?", answered from one fixed page
"Email me a reminder the day before each of my bookings", sent on a schedule
"I need 20 acrylic parts by Friday, so what machine, training and slots do I need?"

items.stem: Name one advantage a fixed workflow has over an agent when the steps of a task are known in advance.
